Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN)  -- Colombian officials are blaming the FARC guerrilla group for a car bombing late Sunday at a police station in Cali that killed two people and wounded at least 14. Residents check out a destroyed police building after a car bombing Sunday night in Cali, Colombia. It was the second bombing in Colombia attributed to the Marxist guerrilla group in less than a week. An explosion at a Blockbuster video rental store in an upscale Bogota neighborhood Tuesday killed two and wounded more than 20. The suspect in Sunday night's attack was killed in a shootout with police after the explosion, Cali Mayor Jorge Ivan Ospina said Monday, hours after convening a special security meeting in the middle of the night. "Although the explosive device only had moderate impact," Ospina said on the Cali government Web site, "we should not forget we are at war and the FARC has been committing terrorist acts in Bogota, Neiva, Cali and other cities in the country. That's why we cannot let our guard down, since they take advantage of Sundays and city centers, where control is more difficult." The explosion came just hours after the rebel group released four hostages in what many interpreted as a gesture to reach a peace accord with the government. Two officials also are slated to be released this week. FARC, which is the Spanish acronym for Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, is the largest and oldest revolutionary group in the nation and has been at war with the government for more than 40 years. According to Ospina, a blue and red Renault 12 Break pickup crashed into the police headquarters in Cali at 10:38 p.m. and then exploded. The driver tried to flee but was felled by two shots from uniformed police and died a few hours later at a hospital, the mayor said. The explosion caused damage in a two-block area, the Cali news Web site Semana.com said. Five of the 14 wounded were minors, Ospina said, citing emergency director Laureano Quintero. The injured are suffering from fractures and other wounds not considered life-threatening, he said. Cali's health minister, Alejandro Varela, said earlier 32 were wounded, including a pregnant woman who was in good condition. Others complained of hearing problems. The mayor's office said the previous higher tally could be a result of people not wounded in the bombing but seeking medical attention to receive government help. Three police were wounded, including a major with a broken arm and an officer who had to have three fingers amputated on his left hand, said the police chief, Gustavo Adolfo Ricaurte Tapia. The bombing caused a temporary power outage, which made security more difficult for officials, said the news Web site Burladero.com. It was the fourth bombing in Cali in less than 42 months, Semana.com said. The latest bombing took place about five blocks from the Palace of Justice, which was blasted by a car bomb in August, killing four and wounding 26. Police buildings were bombed in April 2007 and August 2006. The earlier blast killed five and wounded 17, Semana.com said. Security analysts say FARC has about 9,000 to 12,000 armed guerillas and several thousand supporters, mostly in rural areas. The guerrilla group was established in 1964 as the military wing of the Colombian Communist Party. The guerrillas operate mostly in Colombia but have carried out extortion, kidnappings and other activities in Venezuela, Panama and Ecuador, according to the Federation of American Scientists Intelligence Resource Program. Authorities said Sunday night's bomb contained 90 kilograms (198 pounds) of ammonium nitrate fertilizer and fuel, a commonly used explosive, Semana.com said. By comparison, the bomb that Timothy McVeigh used in the 1995 bombing in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, contained more than 2,800 kilos (6,200 pounds) of ammonium nitrate and diesel fuel.

Two additional officials are scheduled for release this week. FARC—the Spanish acronym for the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia—stands as the nation's largest and oldest revolutionary movement, having waged war against the government for more than four decades.

According to Ospina, a blue and red Renault 12 Break pickup truck crashed into the Cali police headquarters at 10:38 p.m. before detonating. The driver attempted to flee but was struck down by two shots from uniformed police and died several hours later at a hospital, the mayor reported. This marked the fourth bombing in Cali within less than 42 months, Semana.com reported. The latest attack occurred roughly five blocks from the Palace of Justice, which was struck by a car bomb in August, killing four and wounding 26. Police facilities had previously been bombed in April 2007 and August 2006, with the earlier blast claiming five lives and injuring 17, according to Semana.com.

# Colombia Attributes Cali Police Station Attack to FARC Rebels

**BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN)** -- Authorities in Colombia are pointing to the FARC guerrilla organization as responsible for Sunday night's car bomb attack on a Cali police station, an incident that claimed two lives and left at least 14 people injured.

This marked the second bombing within a week linked to the Marxist rebel faction. Just days earlier, on Tuesday, an explosion at a Blockbuster store in a wealthy Bogota district had killed two people and injured over 20 others.

Cali's mayor, Jorge Ivan Ospina, announced Monday—following an emergency middle-of-the-night security session—that police had killed the suspected bomber during an exchange of gunfire after the blast. Speaking through the city government's website, Ospina noted, "Even though this particular device caused relatively limited damage, we must remember our nation remains in conflict, with FARC continuing its terrorist campaign across Bogota, Neiva, Cali, and other urban centers. Vigilance cannot lapse, as these groups exploit Sunday timing and city centers where oversight proves more challenging."

Notably, the attack occurred mere hours after the rebels had freed four hostages—a move many viewed as a step toward potential peace negotiations with the government. Additionally, two more captives are expected to be freed this week.

FARC—the Spanish abbreviation standing for Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia—represents the country's largest and longest-standing insurgent movement, having fought government forces for over four decades.

Mayor Ospina detailed how a red-and-blue Renault 12 Break pickup truck rammed into Cali's police headquarters at 10:38 p.m. before detonating. The driver attempted to escape but was shot twice by officers in uniform, later succumbing to his injuries at a local hospital.

According to the Cali-based news outlet Semana.com, the blast damaged buildings spanning two city blocks. Ospina, citing emergency services director Laureano Quintero, reported that five of the 14 injured victims were minors, with injuries including fractures that were not deemed life-threatening.

Earlier reports from Cali's health minister, Alejandro Varela, had put the injury count at 32, including a pregnant woman described as stable. Some victims reported hearing damage. Mayor's office officials suggested the initial higher figure may have included individuals who weren't actually hurt in the explosion but sought medical treatment anyway to access government assistance programs.

Police Chief Gustavo Adolfo Ricaurte Tapia confirmed three officers were among the injured—a major suffered a broken arm, while another officer required amputation of three fingers on his left hand.

The explosion triggered a temporary blackout, complicating security efforts, according to the news site Burladero.com. Semana.com noted this represented the fourth bombing incident in Cali within roughly 42 months.

The attack site sits approximately five blocks from the Palace of Justice, which suffered its own car bombing in August that killed four and injured 26. Additional police facility bombings occurred in April 2007 and August 2006, with the earlier incident causing five deaths and 17 injuries, per Semana.com.

Security experts estimate FARC's ranks include somewhere between 9,000 and 12,000 armed fighters, supported by several thousand sympathizers concentrated in rural regions. Founded in 1964 as the armed wing of Colombia's Communist Party, the group primarily operates within Colombian borders but has also engaged in kidnapping, extortion, and other criminal activities in neighboring Venezuela, Panama, and Ecuador, according to data from the Federation of American Scientists Intelligence Resource Program.

Regarding the explosive materials used, Semana.com reported that Sunday's device contained approximately 90 kilograms (198 pounds) of ammonium nitrate fertilizer combined with fuel—a widely available explosive combination. For context, this amount pales in comparison to the more than 2,800 kilograms (6,200 pounds) of similar materials Timothy McVeigh used in the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing.

**CALI, Colombia** — A powerful car bomb exploded outside a police station in this southwestern Colombian city, killing at least several people and injuring dozens more, authorities said. Colombian officials quickly attributed the attack to the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, known as FARC, the country's largest leftist guerrilla group.

The explosion tore through a busy commercial district near the police facility, shattering windows in nearby buildings, damaging vehicles, and sending plumes of black smoke into the sky. Emergency crews rushed to the scene as police cordoned off the area, searching for secondary devices — a tactic sometimes used by armed groups in Colombia to target first responders.

"This was a cowardly attack aimed at civilians and the institutions that protect them," a senior police official told reporters at the scene. "We are working to determine the exact explosive materials used and how the vehicle was positioned."

Colombia's Defense Ministry said preliminary evidence — including the type of explosives and the tactical signature of the attack — pointed to FARC involvement. The group has a long history of using car bombs and improvised explosive devices against security forces, particularly in urban centers such as Cali, Medellín, and Bogotá.

Witnesses described a chaotic scene in the moments after the blast.

"I heard a deafening noise and then everything went dark with smoke," said one nearby shop owner. "People were screaming, running in every direction. It was terrifying."

Ambulances transported the wounded to area hospitals, some of which reported being overwhelmed by the influx of patients. Local officials urged residents to avoid the area as investigators worked to secure the scene and gather evidence.

Cali's mayor condemned the attack and vowed that the city would not be intimidated. "We will not allow violence to dictate the future of our city," the mayor said in a brief statement. "Our security forces remain committed to protecting the people of Cali."

The bombing comes amid a period of heightened tension in Colombia's decades-long conflict with FARC, one of the oldest and most prominent guerrilla movements in Latin America. Though the group has been engaged in on-and-off peace negotiations with the Colombian government over the years, splinter factions and hardline elements have continued to carry out attacks against police and military targets, particularly in rural and semi-urban areas where the group maintains influence.

Colombian President's office issued a statement condemning the attack "in the strongest terms," calling it "an attack not just on the police, but on all Colombians who seek peace."

# Car Bomb Explodes at Police Station in Colombia, Officials Blame Dissident FARC Faction

**BOGOTÁ, Colombia (AP)** — A car bomb detonated outside a police station in southwestern Colombia early Wednesday, wounding at least 14 people and causing significant structural damage in the latest attack authorities have linked to dissident factions of the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC).

The explosion occurred around 5:30 a.m. local time in the municipality of Corinto, in the Cauca department, a region long considered a stronghold for armed groups involved in drug trafficking and illegal mining operations. Colombia's Defense Ministry said the vehicle, packed with an estimated 80 kilograms of explosives, was detonated near the entrance of the police compound.

"This was a direct attack against the institutions that protect our communities," said Defense Minister Iván Velásquez during a press conference in Bogotá. "We will not allow armed groups to dictate the future of our territories through violence and intimidation."

Local authorities reported that the blast damaged at least a dozen nearby homes and businesses, shattering windows and collapsing part of a wall at a nearby school, though classes were not in session at the time. Corinto Mayor Oscar Losada described the scene as "chaotic," with residents rushing to help the wounded before ambulances arrived.

"We heard the explosion from kilometers away," Losada said. "This community has already suffered so much from this conflict, and yet here we are again."

## FARC Dissidents Blamed

While no group immediately claimed responsibility, Colombian military officials pointed to dissident factions of FARC — specifically a faction known as the Segunda Marquetalia, led by former guerrilla commanders who rejected the 2016 peace accords. General Helder Giraldo, commander of Colombia's armed forces, said intelligence reports indicated the attack was likely retaliation for recent military operations targeting cocaine production facilities in the region.

"These groups continue to operate under the guise of revolutionary ideology, but their true motivation is protecting drug trafficking routes," Giraldo said.

FARC, once Latin America's largest rebel group, waged a decades-long insurgency against the Colombian state beginning in 1964, rooted in demands for land reform and rural economic justice. The conflict, which also involved right-wing paramilitary groups and government forces, killed more than 260,000 people and displaced millions before the historic 2016 peace deal, signed under then-President Juan Manuel Santos, led to the disarmament of roughly 13,000 fighters.

However, an estimated 3,000 to 5,000 fighters have since regrouped into dissident factions, according to Colombia's Ombudsman's Office, rejecting the peace process and continuing to control lucrative drug trafficking corridors, particularly in Cauca, Nariño, and parts of the Amazon region bordering Venezuela.

## Renewed Violence Amid Peace Talks

The attack comes as President Gustavo Petro's government continues to pursue its "Total Peace" policy, an ambitious effort to negotiate simultaneously with multiple armed groups, including FARC dissident factions and the National Liberation Army (ELN). Critics argue the strategy has allowed armed groups to regroup and expand territorial control even as talks continue.

"This bombing shows the limits of a peace policy that hasn't translated into security on the ground," said Sergio Guzmán, director of Colombia Risk Analysis, a Bogotá-based consultancy. "Communities in Cauca are paying the price for a strategy that has yet to produce concrete results."

Human Rights Watch has documented a rise in attacks attributed to dissident groups over the past two years, including targeted killings of social leaders, extortion of local businesses, and forced recruitment of minors in rural areas.

Colombia's Attorney General's Office said it has opened an investigation into Wednesday's bombing and deployed additional forensic teams to the scene. President Petro condemned the attack in a post on social media, calling it "a cowardly act against the Colombian people" and pledging to reinforce security operations in Cauca.

As of Wednesday evening, none of the injuries were reported as life-threatening, though local hospitals said several victims remained in critical condition. Authorities have not released the names of the wounded, several of whom were reportedly police officers stationed at the facility.

The attack marks at least the third car bombing targeting security forces in Colombia this year, underscoring the fragile security situation even as the government continues efforts to end nearly six decades of armed conflict.
